subject: Banking
title: The National Banking Act
description: A short lesson to help you apply The National Banking Act.

hook.text: In 1863, Lincoln signed the National Banking Act. America finally got a uniform currency and federal bank charters.

buildup.text: The Civil War needed funding. National banks could buy government bonds and issue standardized banknotes against them.

discovery.text: The act taxed state banknotes out of existence. One national currency replaced thousands of wildcat currencies.

twist.text: State banks survived by inventing checking accounts. They didn't need to issue notes if customers wrote checks instead.

climax.text: The National Banking Act unified American money. But it also funded a war, proving what central banking was really for.

punchline.text: Lincoln unified American currency. The real goal was funding the Civil War.

quiz.question: What was the primary purpose of the National Banking Act?
options: Fund the Civil War through standardized banking

details.summary: The National Banking Acts of 1863 and 1864 created a unified US banking system by establishing nationally chartered banks, a national currency, and federal bank supervision, replacing the chaotic system of thousands of competing state banknotes.
details.whyItMatters: The National Banking Act created the federal banking framework that still exists today. It solved the problem of thousands of different banknotes and established the principle of federal bank oversight that the Fed later built upon.
takeaways: The acts created nationally chartered banks supervised by the OCC
A uniform national currency replaced thousands of state banknotes
The dual banking system of federal and state charters persists today

faq.question: What problem did the National Banking Act solve?
faq.answer: Before 1863, over 7,000 state-chartered banks issued their own banknotes, creating a chaotic system where note values varied by issuing bank reputation. The act created a single national currency and federal supervision for banks choosing national charters.

faq.question: Why does the US still have both state and national bank charters?
faq.answer: The dual system survived because states resisted losing banking oversight authority. Today, banks can choose state or national charters with different regulators and rules, creating what critics call regulatory arbitrage and defenders call regulatory competition.
